title: State settles Key Bridge suit for $2.25 billion; Dali owners face criminal charges
summary: Federal prosecutors unsealed a criminal indictment Tuesday against the owners and operators of the cargo ship Dali, for its role in the collapse of the Francis Scott Key Bridge, the same day state officials reached a $2.25 billion lawsuit settlement in the case.
content:
by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters May 12, 2026

by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters May 12, 2026

Federal prosecutors unsealed a criminal indictment Tuesday against the owners and operators of the cargo ship Dali, charging them with conspiracy to defraud the government and with causing the deaths of six workers in the collapse of the Francis Scott Key Bridge.

The announcement came the same day that Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown said the state had reached a $2.25 billion settlement of its lawsuit against the ship’s owner for the bridge collapse that he said in a written statement sent “shockwaves through Maryland and caused damages on a scale this state had never seen.”

The settlement and the indictment represent just some of the legal actions against the companies behind the Dali, the 900-foot fully loaded container ship that lost power early on the morning of March 26, 2024, and crashed into the Key Bridge. The bridge collapsed in an instant, killing six members of a road crew who were working on the bridge, pinning the ship and blocking the Patapsco River channel, closing the Port of Baltimore for 11 weeks.

Prosecutors with the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Baltimore said that company officials were aware of hazardous conditions onboard the Dali well before the crash.

“As laid out in this indictment, this collapse should have never happened,” said Jim Paul, special agent in charge for the FBI Baltimore field office said Tuesday. “As alleged, the bridge was struck and collapsed because those who were responsible for the ship’s operations deliberately cut corners at the expense of safety.”

Federal officials unsealed the indictment on board the NS Savannah, which overlooks the remnants of the Key Bridge. The indictment had been returned by a federal grand jury Friday against Synergy Marine Private Ltd. and Synergy Maritime Private Ltd.

U.S. Attorney for Maryland Kelly O. Hayes said the indictment alleges that the ship was using an improper fuel pump system that led it to lose power and crash into the bridge.

Hayes said the Dali lost power twice on the morning of March 26, 2024, as it was leaving the Seagirt Terminal. She said the first time the ship lost power was likely due to a faulty wire and power was quickly restored through automatic backup systems. The power went out again moments later, due to an improper fueling system that was supposed to keep generators supplied with fuel, and it was then that crew members lost control of the ship and allided with the bridge.

“The second loss of power happened because the defendants relied on a flushing pump to supply fuel to two of the Dali’s generators,” Hayes said.

She said the flushing pump did not automatically restart once power was restored after the first power outage, and a manual restart did not occur in time to avoid a second outage.

“After that first blackout, the ship’s two running generators became starved of fuel, causing a second blackout,” she said. “As alleged in the indictment, the use of the flushing pump … was a hazardous condition under U.S. Coast Guard regulation and a violation of international law.”

State to ‘off ramp’ Key Bridge contractor as work continues

She said that the companies had allegedly used the flushing pump systems on three ships, including the Dali, since 2020, and took steps to hide that fact “both before and after the crash.”

Radhakrishnan Karthik Nair, a technical superintendent who worked with both companies, is alleged to have lied to federal transportation officials when he told them he was unaware of the flushing pump system used on the Dali, according to the indictment. It also said Synergy employees fabricated safety inspections and certifications of the vessel, and presented the false safety certifications to the National Transportation Safety Board and a federal grand jury in Baltimore.

“All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty at a trial beyond reasonable doubt,” Hayes said. “We look forward to pursuing our case in trial.”

In response to reporters’ questions, Hayes said that federal officials hope the shipping industry will “take note of this indictment,” but she could not comment on whether there were investigations ongoing related to other vessels with similar hazardous safety concerns.

The indictment says that the defendants caused at least $5 billion in gross  losses in the crash, and the shipping company could be on the hook for twice that amount if the federal prosecutors are successful.

The Maryland Attorney General’s office, meanwhile, announced the last settlement with Grace Ocean Private Ltd. and Synergy Marine Pte Ltd., owner and operator of the Dali, resolving the 2024 lawsuit by state officials against the shipping companies, according to a Tuesday news release.

Brown had announced settlement in principle with the ship’s operators and owners in April. The agreement was finalized Tuesday, he said in the release.

The  press release said that a legal action continues against Hyundai Heavy Industries, the company that built the Dali. In a 2025 report by the NTSB, the federal officials found the shipbuilders to be at fault for causing the ship’s loss of power.

“This $2.25 billion settlement reflects the full measure of accountability we were able to secure from the vessel interests — and our pursuit of justice is not finished,” Brown said. “We will continue to press our claims against the shipbuilder whose fault helped bring this bridge down.”
